summary: This informational RFC explores application scenarios and use cases for low-power wireless personal area networks, and lays out design space dimensions. It lists market domains that motivate the 6LoWPAN work.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a list of where tiny wireless gadgets might be used and what they need. It helps decide how to design the rules for them.

questions: iot application scenarios low power wireless
subtitle: Applying IPv6 to power-constrained wireless sensor networks

tldr.problem: Wireless sensor networks have extreme resource constraints: tiny processors, limited memory, battery power, and lossy connections. These networks need IPv6 addressing but face challenges in how to deploy it.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC explores the design space for 6LoWPAN deployments by categorizing networks along nine dimensions: how they are deployed, their size, power sources, connectivity patterns, hop requirements, traffic types, security needs, mobility, and quality-of-service requirements.
tldr.outcome: The document identifies six major application scenarios—industrial monitoring, structural health, home automation, healthcare, vehicle telematics, and agriculture—showing that 6LoWPAN is well-suited for a broad range of real-world IoT deployments.

facts.label: Typical memory
facts.value: Kilobytes of RAM, tens of kilobytes of flash

today: RFC 6568 remains informational and has not been obsoleted. The 6LoWPAN standards and protocols described in its references are still in active use for IoT and wireless sensor network deployments, though the specific applications and market domains have evolved as IoT adoption has grown.

sections.title: What Is 6LoWPAN
sections.content:
6LoWPAN stands for IPv6 over Low-power Wireless Personal Area Networks. A LoWPAN is a network built from devices that follow the IEEE 802.15.4 standard, a specification for short-range, low-power wireless radios.

These devices face severe constraints. The smallest LoWPAN nodes have 8-bit processors running at about 10 MHz, just a few kilobytes of RAM, and batteries that must last months or years. Radio ranges are typically tens of meters. Data rates max out at 250 kilobits per second, often much lower. Despite these limits, these networks need to send data reliably to the internet. 6LoWPAN protocols compress and adapt IPv6 to work under these conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: Tiny wireless gadgets with very little power and memory need to talk to each other and the internet using IPv6. LoWPAN is the name for networks of these gadgets, and 6LoWPAN is how to run IPv6 on them even though they are so small.

sections.title: The Design Space
sections.content:
The RFC catalogs nine dimensions that characterize how a LoWPAN can be organized. Each dimension captures a choice that affects the network's structure and the protocols it needs.

Deployment ranges from scattered (random placement) to carefully planned (organized locations), and can happen all at once or gradually. Network Size can be as small as a dozen nodes, reach hundreds, or scale to thousands. Power Source varies: some networks run entirely on batteries, others mix battery-powered sensors with mains-powered relay nodes, or harvest energy from solar cells. Connectivity can be always-on, intermittent (regular sleep periods), or sporadic (mostly disconnected, brief windows of connection). Multi-Hop Communication measures how many hops data must traverse: simple star topologies need only one, while mesh networks need many. Traffic Pattern describes the flow: point-to-multipoint (one sensor to many controllers), multipoint-to-point (many sensors to one aggregator), or point-to-point (peer communication). Security Level ranges from lightweight checks to full encryption and authentication. Mobility can be none, controlled (planned movement), or unpredictable. Quality of Service defines delivery requirements, from loose tolerances for periodic readings to strict demands for real-time alarms.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks can be designed in many different ways depending on what they do. Some have lots of small gadgets, others just a few. Some run on batteries forever, others plug in. Some need fast messages, others are OK with slow ones. The memo lists all the big choices and how they affect the design.

sections.title: Six Real-World Applications
sections.content:
The RFC describes six concrete scenarios showing how 6LoWPAN applies to actual problems. Industrial Monitoring uses sensors to track temperature, vibration, and energy use in factories and warehouses, replacing manual inspection with automated alerts. Structural Monitoring watches bridges, buildings, and tunnels for signs of damage, placing sensors on pillars and measuring vibrations to catch problems early. Connected Home applications range from security (door sensors, motion detectors) to climate control and energy management, letting homeowners monitor and manage systems remotely. Healthcare systems attach wearable sensors to patients to track heart rate and movement, enabling home care and early warnings of health changes. Vehicle Telematics embeds sensors in roads to track vehicle speed and position for traffic management and safety. Agricultural Monitoring deploys sensors across fields to measure soil moisture, temperature, and sunlight, automatically triggering irrigation or alerting farmers to pests.

Each scenario has distinct requirements. Industrial systems demand reliable, time-critical event notifications and strong security. Agricultural networks tolerate longer delays but need to cover large areas and handle sensor failure gracefully. Healthcare systems require encryption for privacy and rapid response to abnormal readings. These variety of demands show why a single network design cannot fit all uses.
sections.plainLanguage: A hospital keeps blood packs at exactly the right temperature by watching with wireless sensors. A vineyard measures soil moisture and sun to decide when to water. A building watches for fires and shakes that mean danger. A home automation system lets you turn lights on from your phone. Each has different rules about speed, security, and how many gadgets are involved.

sections.title: How These Networks Are Built
sections.content:
6LoWPAN networks can be assembled in two main ways. Route-over architecture uses the LoWPAN nodes themselves as routers, creating a multi-hop mesh where each node forwards packets using IP routing. Mesh-under architecture handles multi-hop forwarding below the IP layer, keeping the local link-local scope across the entire LoWPAN. Both approaches work with 6LoWPAN; the choice depends on the application.

At the boundary of the LoWPAN, a Border Router (LBR) connects the sensor network to the outside world, usually the internet. A Local Controller (LC) acts as a data aggregator, collecting information from leaf nodes, performing early filtering or processing, and coordinating responses. In large networks, multiple LCs may be deployed to balance load.

Each node obtains an IPv6 address through a lightweight neighbor discovery process adapted from the standard IPv6 procedure. Nodes use link-local addresses for communication within the LoWPAN and may obtain globally routable addresses for communication with external networks through the LBR.
sections.plainLanguage: Gadgets can talk directly to each other (mesh) or through special relay gadgets. At the edge, a special box (the border router) connects the whole network to the internet. Some gadgets collect data from others and send it onward, acting like post offices.

sections.title: Security and Practical Challenges
sections.content:
LoWPANs face severe security threats. Devices are often physically exposed outdoors or in untrusted spaces, making them vulnerable to capture, tampering, or destruction. Radio signals can be jammed or eavesdropped. An attacker could modify sensor readings (e.g., turning off a fire alarm) or inject false data to trigger wasteful actions (e.g., flooding a field unnecessarily).

Security must be lightweight because LoWPAN devices lack the power or memory for heavy cryptography. Link-layer encryption, IPsec, or application-layer security can all be used, but the choice depends on the scenario. Industrial and structural monitoring systems often need the strongest security because failures can endanger lives or cost money. Healthcare systems require encryption for privacy. Home automation may tolerate weaker security for non-critical sensors like humidity monitors but demand it for door locks. Agricultural networks may use simple shared-key management or no security at all if the data is non-sensitive.

Management overhead is also significant. Networks must support dynamic node addition and removal, handle node failures gracefully, and provide operators with visibility into the network's health without consuming excessive bandwidth or power.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad people might try to break sensors, trick them, or jam their signals. Because the gadgets have almost no power, they can only use simple security tricks, not heavy locks. So the designer picks which rules matter most: speed, security, or battery life. A blood storage room needs strong locks. A farm temperature sensor does not.
